title: Evaluating agents and RAG systems
summary: Multi-stage systems need stage-by-stage evaluation. For RAG, score retrieval (recall, nDCG on labelled passages) separately from the answer's faithfulness and correctness, and use the pair to locate a failure. For agents, grade the outcome by checking the final state in code, check the trajectory for appropriate tools, valid arguments, forbidden actions and step count, and run each task several times: pass@k (at least one success in k) suits generate-and-test, while pass^k (all k succeed, roughly pᵏ) measures the reliability users experience. Offline suites run on every change; graded production traces feed new failures back into them.
llm_link: Agent and RAG behaviour is sampled from a next-token distribution, so the same task can succeed and fail on different runs. Reliability is a property you measure across runs, not one you observe once.
key_ideas: RAG: evaluate retrieval (recall@k, nDCG) and generation (faithfulness to the retrieved text, correctness) separately. Right passage retrieved + wrong answer → fix generation; never retrieved → fix retrieval.
Agent outcomes: check the state of the world in code (tests pass, the row exists, the calendar entry is on the right day), not the agent's claim of success.
Trajectory checks: allowed tools, valid arguments, no forbidden or premature actions, sensible step count. They catch dangerous routes to a correct outcome.
pass@k = 1 − C(n − c, k)/C(n, k): at least one of k attempts succeeds. pass^k = C(c, k)/C(n, k): all k succeed, ≈ pᵏ for independent attempts (used in τ-bench, Yao et al., 2024).
The eval cycle: an offline regression suite on every change, continuous grading of sampled production traces, and new failures added back to the suite.

quiz.q: A RAG answer is wrong, but the passage containing the right answer was among the retrieved results. Where should you look first?
options: Generation: the prompt, the context packing or the model's use of the passage
quiz.explain: Retrieval did its job. The failure happened when the answer was written: the passage may have been buried mid-context, truncated, or ignored.

quiz.q: An agent reports 'All tests pass, bug fixed.' How should an eval grade the outcome?
options: Run the test suite itself and check the result
quiz.explain: Outcome checks should inspect the actual final state with code. Agents can be wrong about, or misreport, their own success.

quiz.q: Predict the result: an agent succeeds on a task 90% of the time, independently per attempt. What is pass^5, the chance that five attempts all succeed?
quiz.explain: 0.9⁵ ≈ 0.59. pass@5 (at least one success) would be 1 − 0.1⁵ ≈ 0.99999; the two measures answer very different questions.

quiz.q: An agent reached the right final state but issued a refund before checking the order. Which kind of check catches this?
quiz.explain: The outcome looked fine; the path was unsafe. Trajectory checks examine which tools were called, in what order and with what arguments.

quiz.q: For an assistant that customers rely on every day, which reliability metric matters more?
options: pass@k: at least one of k attempts works
quiz.explain: A user does not get to keep the best of k tries. Consistency across repeated runs, pass^k, is the experience they have.

problems.title: Find where a RAG answer broke
problems.prompt:
Each eval case records the ids that retrieval returned, the ids labelled relevant, and whether the final answer was graded correct. Write diagnose(case):

  • "ok" if the answer was correct;
  • "retrieval" if it was wrong and no relevant passage was retrieved;
  • "generation" if it was wrong although a relevant passage was retrieved.

Then write tally(cases) returning a dict with counts for all three labels (including zeros), and run it on CASES. Which stage should you fix first?
problems.starter:
CASES = [
    {"retrieved": ["p1", "p2"], "relevant": ["p1"], "correct": True},
    {"retrieved": ["p3", "p4"], "relevant": ["p9"], "correct": False},
    {"retrieved": ["p5", "p6"], "relevant": ["p6"], "correct": False},
    {"retrieved": ["p7"],       "relevant": ["p8"], "correct": False},
    {"retrieved": ["p2", "p1"], "relevant": ["p2"], "correct": True},
]

def diagnose(case):
    # TODO: 'ok', 'retrieval' or 'generation'
    pass


def tally(cases):
    counts = {"ok": 0, "retrieval": 0, "generation": 0}
    # TODO: count diagnose(c) for every case
    return counts

tests.name: missing passage means retrieval
tests.code: assert diagnose(CASES[1])=='retrieval', f'no relevant id was retrieved, got {diagnose(CASES[1])}'

tests.name: retrieved but wrong means generation
tests.code: assert diagnose(CASES[2])=='generation', f'p6 was retrieved yet the answer is wrong, got {diagnose(CASES[2])}'

tests.name: tally counts every label
tests.code:
r=tally(CASES)
assert r=={'ok':2,'retrieval':2,'generation':1}, f'expected ok 2, retrieval 2, generation 1, got {r}'

problems.title: pass@k versus pass^k
problems.prompt:
You ran a task n times and c runs succeeded. Write the two unbiased estimators:

pass_at_k(n, c, k)  = 1 - C(n - c, k) / C(n, k)   # at least one of k succeeds
pass_hat_k(n, c, k) = C(c, k) / C(n, k)           # all k succeed

where C is math.comb (it returns 0 when asked to choose more items than there are). Then compare them for n = 10, c = 8 as k grows from 1 to 5: one rises, the other falls.
problems.starter:
from math import comb

def pass_at_k(n, c, k):
    # TODO: chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds
    pass


def pass_hat_k(n, c, k):
    # TODO: chance that all k attempts succeed
    pass

tests.name: k = 1 is the success rate
tests.code: assert abs(pass_at_k(10,8,1)-0.8)<1e-9 and abs(pass_hat_k(10,8,1)-0.8)<1e-9, f'with k=1 both equal c/n = 0.8, got {pass_at_k(10,8,1)}, {pass_hat_k(10,8,1)}'

tests.name: the two diverge as k grows
tests.code:
a=[pass_at_k(10,8,k) for k in range(1,6)]; h=[pass_hat_k(10,8,k) for k in range(1,6)]
assert all(x<=y for x,y in zip(a,a[1:])) and all(x>=y for x,y in zip(h,h[1:])) and h[-1]<0.25, f'pass@k should rise and pass^k fall (to about 0.22 at k=5); got {a} and {h}'

tests.name: too few successes
tests.code:
assert pass_hat_k(10,2,3)==0, 'with only 2 successes, 3 attempts cannot all succeed'
assert pass_at_k(10,10,3)==1, 'with every run successful, pass@k is 1'

hints: math.comb(n, k) counts the ways to choose k of n.
pass_at_k: 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)

problems.title: Check an agent's trajectory
problems.prompt:
Write check_trajectory(calls, allowed, forbidden, max_steps, needs_before). calls is a list of {"tool": ..., "args": ...} in order. Return a list of problem strings (empty if the path is fine):

  • more calls than max_steps;
  • a call to a tool in forbidden, or to one not in allowed;
  • a call to a tool t listed in needs_before before the tool needs_before[t] has been called, e.g. {"issue_refund": "lookup_order"}.

Mention the step number (starting at 1) in each problem so a reviewer can find it.
problems.starter:
def check_trajectory(calls, allowed, forbidden, max_steps, needs_before):
    problems = []
    # TODO 1: too many steps
    # TODO 2: for each step: forbidden tools, tools not in allowed
    # TODO 3: a tool used before the tool it needs_before
    return problems

tests.name: a clean path
tests.code:
C=[{'tool':'lookup_order','args':{}},{'tool':'issue_refund','args':{}}]
r=check_trajectory(C,{'lookup_order','issue_refund'},set(),5,{'issue_refund':'lookup_order'})
assert r==[], f'expected no problems, got {r}'

tests.name: refund before lookup
tests.code:
C=[{'tool':'issue_refund','args':{}},{'tool':'lookup_order','args':{}}]
r=check_trajectory(C,{'lookup_order','issue_refund'},set(),5,{'issue_refund':'lookup_order'})
assert len(r)==1 and '1' in r[0] and 'lookup_order' in r[0], f'expected one problem at step 1 naming lookup_order, got {r}'

tests.name: forbidden and unknown tools
tests.code:
C=[{'tool':'delete_account','args':{}},{'tool':'browse','args':{}}]
r=check_trajectory(C,{'lookup_order'},{'delete_account'},5,{})
assert len(r)==2 and 'delete_account' in r[0] and 'browse' in r[1], f'expected a forbidden-tool and a not-allowed problem, got {r}'

tests.name: too many steps
tests.code:
C=[{'tool':'lookup_order','args':{}}]*4
r=check_trajectory(C,{'lookup_order'},set(),3,{})
assert len(r)==1 and '4' in r[0], f'4 steps exceed the limit of 3, got {r}'

hints: if len(calls) > max_steps: problems.append(f'too many steps: {len(calls)} > {max_steps}')
Keep a set `seen` of tools already called; check needs_before before adding the current tool to it.
Use elif so a forbidden tool is not also reported as not allowed.
